title: Accessibility basics: keyboard, contrast, labels
goal: Audit one of your pages for accessibility and fix every issue you find.

concepts: Who accessibility helps: screen reader users, keyboard users, low vision, everyone on a bad phone screen
Keyboard navigation: Tab order, focus styles, never remove outlines without a replacement
Colour contrast: 4.5:1 for normal text
Labels for every form field; buttons vs links
Alt text, heading order, and landmarks
aria-label only when there's no visible text (first rule of ARIA: prefer native HTML)

resources.title: MDN: HTML: A good basis for accessibility

build.task: Copy your Day 11 BrightPath page into day19/. Audit it: (1) unplug or ignore your mouse and use only Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter and Space to reach and use everything; (2) run Lighthouse's Accessibility audit in DevTools; (3) check your text and button colours in the WebAIM contrast checker; (4) check headings form a sensible outline. Record every issue in day19/audit.md (issue, where, fix), fix them all, and re-run Lighthouse. Aim for an Accessibility score of 95+.

# Accessibility audit: BrightPath

Lighthouse accessibility score:

acceptance: audit.md lists at least 5 real issues with fixes, plus before/after Lighthouse scores
Every interactive element is reachable and usable with the keyboard alone, in a logical order
Visible focus style on every link, button and input
All text passes 4.5:1 contrast (large text 3:1)
Every input has a label; icon-only buttons have an accessible name
Lighthouse Accessibility score 95 or higher

hints: Lighthouse is in DevTools (the Lighthouse tab). Untick everything except Accessibility to make it faster.
Common issues: low-contrast grey text, missing form labels, links that say 'click here', images with empty or filename alt text, skipped heading levels, and outline: none on buttons.
Use a <button> for actions and an <a href> for navigation. A div with an onclick can't be reached with Tab.
proof: Commit with day19/audit.md and the fixed page.

explainBack.q: Pick the most serious issue from your audit. Who would it have blocked and how?
lookFor: names a real issue from their audit
identifies the affected group (keyboard, screen reader, low vision)

explainBack.q: Why should you prefer a native <button> over a <div> styled to look like a button?
lookFor: announced as button by screen readers

explainBack.q: What does a 4.5:1 contrast ratio mean and how did you check it?
lookFor: difference in luminance between text and background
used a contrast checker or DevTools

lastHintExplanation: Native HTML elements come with accessibility built in: a <button> is focusable, works with Enter and Space, and is announced as a button. A styled div has none of that. Contrast ratio compares text and background brightness; WCAG AA requires 4.5:1 for normal text so people with low vision or a phone in sunlight can read it.

A page uses
Save
. A keyboard user presses Tab repeatedly. What happens?
options: Focus lands on Save and Enter clicks it
The browser converts it to a button
predict.why: A plain div isn't focusable, so Tab never reaches it.

title: CSS custom properties, a mini design system, and dark mode
goal: Build a small set of reusable design tokens and components, and switch the whole page to dark mode by changing variables.

concepts: Custom properties: --name: value; and var(--name, fallback)
Design tokens: colours, font sizes, spacing scale, radius, shadows
Variables cascade and can be redefined in a smaller scope
prefers-color-scheme media query for dark mode
Reusable component classes: .btn, .btn--primary, .card
Naming: a simple, consistent convention (e.g. BEM-lite)

build.task: In day20/, create tokens.css (all variables), components.css (buttons, cards, inputs, badges built only from variables) and a styleguide.html page that shows every component: primary/secondary/danger buttons in normal, hover and disabled states, a card, a text input with label and error state, and 3 badges. Add dark mode two ways: automatically with prefers-color-scheme, and with a [data-theme="dark"] attribute on <html> that you can toggle by editing the HTML.

starterFiles.name: day20/tokens.css

acceptance: components.css has no hard-coded colours or spacing: everything uses var(--...)
Style guide shows buttons (3 variants with hover and disabled), card, input with error state, badges
Dark mode follows the OS setting via prefers-color-scheme
Adding data-theme="dark" to <html> forces dark mode
Both themes pass contrast checks for body text and buttons

hints: Only tokens.css should contain raw colour values. If you see #hex in components.css, move it into a token.
Dark mode is just redefining the tokens: @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) { :root { --color-bg: #0f172a; --color-text: #e2e8f0 } } and :root[data-theme="dark"] { ...same... }.
Disabled buttons: .btn:disabled { opacity: .5; cursor: not-allowed }. Use a real disabled attribute so it can't be clicked.
proof: Commit with day20/ files and screenshots of light and dark modes.

explainBack.q: Explain how your dark mode works without changing any component CSS.
lookFor: dark mode redefines the variable values
cascade: new values apply everywhere they're used

explainBack.q: What is a design token and why is a spacing scale useful?

lastHintExplanation: Components only reference variables, like background: var(--color-bg). Dark mode simply redefines those variables on :root (via prefers-color-scheme or [data-theme=dark]), and because custom properties cascade, every component picks up the new values with no component changes. Tokens are named design decisions that keep a UI consistent.

predict.q: :root { --c: red } .box { --c: blue } .box p { color: var(--c) }. What colour is a p inside .box?
predict.why: Custom properties inherit; the nearest definition (.box) wins.

predict.q: p { color: var(--missing) } with --missing never defined, and the parent's color is green. What colour is the p?
options: Green (inherited, because the value is invalid at computed time)
predict.why: An undefined variable makes the declaration invalid at computed-value time, so color falls back to inherited (green).

dsa.note: Modify the array without creating a new one. Draw the array after each step.

questions.q: A father is 3 times as old as his son. In 10 years he will be twice as old. How old is the son now?
A and B's ages add up to 50. Five years ago their ages were in the ratio 3:2. How old is A now?
questions.why: Five years ago their total was 40, split 3:2 as 24 and 16. So A is now 29.

questions.q: P and Q's present ages are in the ratio 4:5. In 6 years the ratio will be 5:6. How old is P?
A mother is 30 years older than her daughter. In 5 years she will be twice the daughter's age. How old is the daughter?
Three children average 9 years old and their ages are in the ratio 2:3:4. How old is the eldest?
questions.why: The total is 27 across 9 parts, so 1 part is 3 and the eldest is 4 × 3 = 12.

Boys and girls are in the ratio 3:2. 20% of boys and 30% of girls hold scholarships. What percent of students do not?

title: Phase 1 project: style the portfolio, mobile-first
goal: Style all four portfolio pages with your own design tokens so they look professional on every screen size.

concepts: Reusing your Day 20 tokens and components
Visual hierarchy: size, weight, colour and space guide the eye
Consistent vertical rhythm with a spacing scale
Styling the active nav link with [aria-current=page]
Checking every page at 360px, 768px and 1280px

resources.title: Refactoring UI: 7 practical tips for cheating at design

build.task: Style the portfolio repo. Copy in your tokens.css and components.css from Day 20 and build style.css on top. Mobile-first: header with a nav that wraps or stacks nicely on phones; hero on index with your name large; project cards in a responsive grid; an about timeline (vertical line with dots using ::before); a styled contact form with focus and error states. Support dark mode. Commit after each page is styled.
acceptance: All 4 pages share one stylesheet set (tokens, components, style) with no inline styles
Looks deliberate at 360px, 768px and 1280px with no horizontal scroll
Active nav link visibly highlighted via [aria-current=page]
Project cards use Grid with auto-fit/minmax
About page timeline built with CSS pseudo-elements
Dark mode works; Lighthouse Accessibility is 95+ on every page

hints: Start from the shared parts (body, header, nav, footer) so every page improves at once. Then do each page's unique sections.

Timeline: .timeline { position: relative; padding-left: 1.5rem; border-left: 2px solid var(--color-border) } .timeline li::before { content: ''; position: absolute; left: -7px; width: 12px; height: 12px; border-radius: 50%; background: var(--color-primary) }. Give each li position: relative and adjust left.
Hierarchy trick: make secondary text smaller and lighter (not just smaller), and add more space between sections than within them.
proof: Link to your portfolio repo's latest commit.

explainBack.q: Show how one of your Day 20 components was reused here. What did reuse save you?
Explain how you built the timeline dots.
lookFor: position absolute inside a relative li

lastHintExplanation: Reusing components means the same .btn and .card classes work on every page, driven by tokens, so a single change updates the whole site. The timeline dots are ::before pseudo-elements (content: '' is required) absolutely positioned inside each relatively positioned list item, sitting on the list's left border.

acceptance: Site is live at https://<username>.github.io/portfolio/
All internal links and images work on the live site (watch for case-sensitive file names)

Every page scores 90+ in all four Lighthouse categories (mobile)

hints: If images work locally but break on GitHub Pages, check capital letters: Me.JPG and me.jpg are different files on the server.
Biggest performance win is usually images: resize to the size actually shown (rarely more than 1600px wide), convert to WebP (squoosh.app), and lazy-load the ones lower on the page.
Pages can take a minute or two to update after a push. Use a private window to avoid seeing a cached version.

explainBack.q: Pick one Lighthouse issue you fixed. What was it and why did your fix improve the score?
Why can GitHub Pages host this site without any server code?
lookFor: server just sends files as they are

lastHintExplanation: A static site is just files; any web server can send them unchanged, which is all GitHub Pages does. Lighthouse's performance score is mostly about how quickly the main content appears, so oversized images are the usual culprit: resizing, using WebP and lazy-loading off-screen images speeds up the first view.

predict.q: Your HTML says but the file is images/photo.jpg. It works on your Windows laptop. What happens on GitHub Pages?
options: Broken image: the server treats names as case-sensitive
predict.why: Most web servers are case-sensitive; Windows and macOS file systems usually aren't.

goal: Prove Phase 1 stuck by building a layout from a text description with no notes, then plan your weak spots.

concepts: Recall practice: building without looking things up first
Spotting your own gaps and writing them down honestly

build.task: Timed challenge (90 minutes, no notes for the first 60): in jobready-journey/day24/, build a 'Recipe page': header with site name and nav; a hero image with the recipe title over it (overlay); a two-column layout on desktop (ingredients list in a sticky sidebar on the left, numbered steps on the right) that stacks on phones; a 'Nutrition' table; 3 related recipe cards in a grid; footer. Commit what you have at 60 minutes with the message 'checkpoint: no notes', then finish with notes. Then write day24/phase1-review.md: what you built without help, what you had to look up, and your top 3 weak topics.
acceptance: A commit named 'checkpoint: no notes' exists, made within 60 minutes
Final page has all listed sections and is responsive with no horizontal scroll at 360px
Sidebar ingredients stay visible while scrolling steps on desktop (sticky)
Hero title is readable over the image (overlay)
phase1-review.md is honest: lists what you looked up and 3 weak topics

hints: Spend the first 5 minutes sketching on paper: which parts are Grid, which are Flexbox, what changes at the breakpoint.
Sticky sidebar: the sidebar needs position: sticky; top: 1rem and must be inside a container taller than itself. align-self: start stops Grid stretching it.
If you get stuck for more than 10 minutes in the no-notes part, write a TODO comment and move on to the next section.
proof: Link to the 'checkpoint: no notes' commit and the final commit.

explainBack.q: What did you have to look up after the checkpoint, and why do you think it didn't stick?
Explain why your sticky sidebar needed align-self: start (or why it worked without it).
lookFor: grid items stretch to row height by default
a stretched item fills the container so it has nowhere to stick

lastHintExplanation: Grid and flex items stretch to fill the row by default. A sidebar stretched to the full height of its container has no room to move, so position: sticky appears to do nothing. align-self: start keeps the sidebar at its natural height so it can stick while the steps scroll past.

predict.q: An element has position: sticky but no top/bottom value. What happens when you scroll?
options: It behaves like normal static flow
predict.why: Sticky needs a threshold like top: 0 to know when to stick.
